title: Police Strength & Police Expenditure
row_label: 16.1.1 The efficiency of the Police force in combating crime, maintenance of law and order and regulating traffic besides numerous other tasks assigned to it from time to time, depends largely on its manpower. Of course, the strength of the police force has to be viewed in relation to the area to be policed, the population to be catered to and the ever growing magnitude of crime incidence in the society. Tables 87 to 91 provide State, UT & City-wise, sex-wise and rank-wise information on ‘Sanctioned’ as well as ‘Actual’ police strength in the country as on 31.12.95. Tables-87, 88 and 91 showed that against the sanctioned strength of 13.2 lakhs of total police force (Civil and Armed combined), the existing (Actual) police strength was 12.5 lakhs, rendering 5.3 per cent of the posts as vacant. Civil Police 16.2.1 The ‘Actual’ strength of Civil Police, including District Armed Police in the country during 1995 was 9,69023 against a ‘Sanctioned’ strength of 10,16,239 (Table-87). Thus the existing Civil Police strength was 95.4 per cent of the sanctioned strength and 4.6 per cent of the posts were vacant. Uttar Pradesh had the highest contingent of civil Police (1,21,012) in the country followed by Maharashtra (1,15,858). The strength of Maharashtra Police declined by 6.6 per cent, compared to the previous year. Of the total Police Strength of 46,681 in the seven Union Territories, Delhi had the largest contingent of 40,212 (86.1%) but at times, even this was found to be inadequate considering the wide variety of tasks it has to perform. Armed Police 16.3.1 The ‘Actual’ strength of Armed Police in the country during 1995 stood at 2,81,987 against the ‘Sanctioned’ strength of 2,99,217. The percentage of unfilled posts in case of Armed Police was more (5.7%) than that of Civil Police (4.6%). The proportion of Armed Police to Civil Police was 1:3.4. The highest contingent of Armed Police (34,143) existed with the State of Uttar Pradesh while there was no sanctioned post for the UTs of Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep. The Armed Police Strength was more than the Civil Police in the North-East States of Manipur, Mizoram and Nagaland. Women Police

Thus, the deficit which was 15.6 per cent in the previous year, rose to 16.5 per cent, in 1995. The proportion of actual ‘Women Civil Police’ to the total ‘Civil Police’ was around 1:63. Among States, the maximum strength of Women Civil Police existed in Maharashtra (2,886) followed by Uttar Pradesh (1,344), Tamil Nadu (1,261), Andhra Pradesh (1,136) and Madhya Pradesh (1053). Ratio of Police to Area and Population

16.5.1 Just as the crime incidence in an area is a deceptive pointer to the crime situation, the absolute strength of police personnel is also not a true indicator for its adequacy to the problem of combating crime and performing the other assigned tasks. The number of policemen per unit area (100 Sq. Kms) and per unit of population (1,000) are considered to be the important factors in planning for their deployment. The State & UT-wise information by various attributes, as also exponentiated to policemen per 1,00,000 population is presented in Table-91.

16.5.2 The strength of police personnel per unit area i.e., per 100 sq.Kms. was 39.5. This recorded an increase of 28.7 per cent in the decade 1985-95 and 5.6 per cent, compared to previous year. However, it should be noted that the area coverage being a constant, the density is expected to progressively increase only. The annual Compound Growth Rate of police strength as also of country’s population maintained relatively the same trend.
